new_statements.quote: Tyhurst (1984) and Mbuagbaw (1994) identified four basic tones in Kenyang: two level tones, high [ ´ ] and low [ ` ], and two contour tones, rising [ ˇ ] and falling [ ˆ ]. Tone wa [sic] represented lexically within morphemes and grammatically within sentences. [...] 4.1 Tonal Contrast. Tones in Kenyang contrast minimally. The speaker uses the pitch of his voice to distinguish lexically between morphemes and words which would have been otherwise identical.

The speaker uses the pitch of his voice to distinguish lexically between morphemes and words which would have been otherwise identical." Mini…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kenyang is described as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (rising, falling), plus downstepped H mentioned later (p. 10-11); tone is contrastive lexically (e.g. [èβá] 'fence' vs [èβà] 'bag', [m̀mú] 'dog' vs [m̀mù] 'person') and grammatically (tense/aspect). The source makes no statement whatsoever about word stress or accent placement; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tone orthography issues (downstep vs high, falling vs low) discussed pp. 10-11.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on morphemes/words (citation forms in minimal pairs) and grammatical tone within sentences; nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1998 lexicon and the SIL materials describe standard (Upper) Kenyang of Manyu Division, Cameroon, as written by the Society for Kenyang Literature; no dialect is specified. Ittmann 1935-36 'Sprache der Nyang' and Glottolog/WALS treat this as the same language (keny1279 / ISO ken; WALS kyg).
